sections.text:
Mark moves fast, and it ends in silence. The women come to the tomb, find it open, hear that Jesus has risen, and flee in trembling and astonishment. “They said nothing to anyone”; they were afraid. The shortest Gospel stops there, and the whole book leans toward that moment.

The pace from the start is quick. Jesus acts with authority: he heals, drives out unclean spirits, calms a storm and forgives sins. The crowds wonder who he is. Halfway through, on the road to the villages of Caesarea Philippi, he asks his disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers, “You are the Christ.” From that point Jesus teaches that he must suffer, die and rise.

The disciples repeatedly fail to understand, even Peter, who tries to rebuke him. More than a third of the book is given to the last week in Jerusalem. At the cross a Roman officer is the one who says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!”

Early tradition says the author was John Mark, writing down the preaching of Peter, probably in Rome. The book is commonly dated to the 60s or around the year 70, and most scholars think it was the first Gospel written.

The oldest copies of Mark end at 16:8, with the women leaving the empty tomb afraid. Verses 9 to 20 appear in later copies, and most Bibles print them with a note. Whether Mark meant to end so abruptly is debated: some hear a deliberate silence that leaves the reader to answer, others suspect that the ending was lost. The book's center is clear either way: who Jesus is cannot be understood apart from the cross.

There is no birth story here and no family tree. Mark starts with a sentence: the beginning of the Good News of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Then comes a voice in the wilderness. John is baptizing at the Jordan, dressed in camel's hair, eating locusts and wild honey, and all Judea and Jerusalem go out to him, confessing their sins. Someone mightier is coming, he says, who will baptize in the Holy Spirit.

Jesus comes from Nazareth and is baptized. The heavens part, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice says, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Immediately the Spirit drives him into the wilderness for forty days of testing by Satan.

After John is taken into custody, Jesus goes to Galilee preaching that God's Kingdom is at hand. He calls Simon, Andrew, James and John from their nets. In Capernaum he teaches with authority and drives an unclean spirit out of a man in the synagogue. He heals many, prays in a quiet place, and touches and heals a man with leprosy.

Mark is usually seen as the earliest Gospel, often dated to around the time of AD 65 to 70. Tradition links it to John Mark and to the preaching of Peter, though many scholars treat the author as unknown. It is the shortest Gospel and moves quickly, often using the word immediately. The messenger passage combines lines from Exodus, Malachi and Isaiah. The unclean spirits recognize who Jesus is before the people do, and Jesus tells them to be quiet. Scholars call this theme the messianic secret.

The house in Capernaum is so full that nobody can get near the door. Four men arrive carrying a paralyzed friend, and they cannot get through the crowd. So they take the roof apart and let him down on his mat in front of Jesus.

Jesus sees their faith and says, “Son, your sins are forgiven you.” Some scribes think in their hearts that this is blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins. Jesus knows it and asks which is easier, to say sins are forgiven or to say, get up and walk. Then he tells the man to rise, and he does, and walks out in front of them all. The crowd is amazed.

Next Jesus calls Levi from the tax office and eats at his house with tax collectors and sinners. When he is questioned, he says the healthy do not need a physician. Asked about fasting, he speaks of a bridegroom, cloth and wineskins. When the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, he mentions David and says the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.

A typical house in Galilee had a flat roof made of beams, branches and packed earth, reached by an outside stair, which is how the men could open it. Levi is called Matthew in the First Gospel; the two names are usually taken to refer to the same person. Tax collectors were disliked because they worked for the Roman system and often took extra. The David story is told in 1 Samuel 21. Mark gives the name of the high priest as Abiathar, while the Old Testament names his father Ahimelech, and readers have explained this in different ways.

In the synagogue there is a man with a withered hand, and people are watching Jesus to see whether he will heal on the Sabbath, so they can accuse him. Jesus tells the man to stand up, then asks the room: is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to kill? Nobody answers. He looks around at them with anger, grieved at their hard hearts, and tells the man to stretch out his hand. It is restored. The Pharisees walk out and begin plotting with the Herodians to destroy him.

Crowds follow him to the sea, and unclean spirits cry out that he is the Son of God. He warns them not to make him known. On a mountain he appoints twelve.

At home his family come to seize him, saying he is insane. Scribes from Jerusalem say he has Beelzebul. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand. When his mother and brothers wait outside, he says that whoever does the will of God is his brother, sister and mother.

The Herodians were supporters of the ruling family of Herod, so an alliance with Pharisees against Jesus was unusual. Mark often places two stories together so that one explains the other. Here the family's concern frames the scribes' accusation. The list of the twelve differs a little from the lists in Matthew and Luke. The warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is read in different ways, but Mark links it directly to the charge that Jesus had an unclean spirit. Christians have long said that those troubled by the passage should not take it as a sentence on themselves.

A great crowd lines the shore of the Sea of Galilee, so many that Jesus steps into a boat and teaches from the water. His story begins with a farmer who went out to sow. Some seed lands on the road, and the birds eat it. Some lands on rocky ground and springs up fast, then is scorched for lack of root. Some falls among thorns and is choked. Some falls on good ground and yields thirty, sixty or one hundred times over.

Later, alone with his followers, Jesus explains. The seed is the word, and the four soils are four ways people respond to it. He adds sayings about a lamp that belongs on a stand, and two more pictures of God’s Kingdom: seed that grows by itself until harvest, and a mustard seed that becomes a large plant.

Then evening comes, and a storm fills the boat while Jesus sleeps on a cushion in the stern. The disciples wake him, asking if he does not care. He speaks to the sea: “Peace! Be still!” The wind stops, and they are left asking who he is.

Mark is usually dated to around the time of the Roman-Jewish war in the first century. Here is the first long block of Jesus’s teaching in the book. A parable is a short story that makes a point by comparison, and Mark says Jesus used them often. Verses 11 and 12 are hard, and Christians read why Jesus spoke in parables in different ways. The Sea of Galilee is a large lake known for sudden storms. Compare the stilling of the sea with Psalm 107:23 to 30.

The boat has barely touched the far shore when a man comes out of the tombs to meet Jesus. He lives there. No chains have held him, and night and day he cries out among the tombs and the mountains. Jesus asks his name, and the answer is “My name is Legion, for we are many.” The spirits beg to be sent into a herd of pigs on the hillside, and the herd rushes into the sea. The people come and find the man sitting, clothed and in his right mind, and they are afraid. They ask Jesus to leave. The man begs to go with him, but is told to go home and tell what the Lord has done.

Back across the lake, Jairus, a synagogue leader, falls at Jesus’s feet for his dying daughter. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his clothes and is healed. Then word comes that the girl has died. Jesus takes her by the hand and says “Talitha cumi!” and the girl, twelve years old, gets up and walks.

The two stories of Jairus’s daughter and the bleeding woman are wrapped together, a pattern Mark uses elsewhere. Under Jewish law of the time, both a long-term bleeding and contact with a dead body made a person ritually unclean, so Jesus’s touch crosses a boundary in each case. Decapolis means ten cities, a region of mostly non-Jewish towns east of the Jordan, so the man’s message goes to a Gentile area. Tombs and pigs also mark this as unclean ground for a Jewish reader.

Jesus comes home. On the Sabbath he teaches in the synagogue, and the town is astonished and then offended: isn’t this the carpenter, Mary’s son? He does few miracles there. He sends the twelve out in pairs with authority over unclean spirits, taking almost nothing, and they preach, heal and cast out demons.

Then Mark stops for a darker story. Herod Antipas had jailed John the Baptist for criticizing his marriage to Herodias. At his birthday banquet he made a rash promise to her daughter, and she asked for John’s head.

The apostles return, and Jesus says, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” The crowd runs ahead. He has compassion on them, and when evening nears he tells the disciples, “You give them something to eat.” Five loaves and two fish feed about five thousand men. That night he walks toward the disciples on the lake, and the wind stops. At Gennesaret people bring the sick to touch his clothes.

This Herod is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee under Rome. He is called king here, though his official title was tetrarch. The shaking off of dust was a gesture of leaving a place that had refused a message. The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle of Jesus told in all four Gospels. Compare John 6. The story echoes Moses and the manna in Exodus 16, and Elisha in 2 Kings 4:42 to 44.

Scribes and Pharisees have come from Jerusalem, and they are watching how the disciples eat. Some eat with unwashed hands, against the tradition of the elders. Jesus turns the question around. They honor tradition and set aside God’s commandment, and he gives the example of Corban, a vow that excuses a person from supporting father or mother.

Then he calls the whole crowd and says that nothing going into a person defiles them, but what comes out does. In the house he explains it to his disciples, and Mark adds that this makes all foods clean. Evil thoughts, theft, murder, deceit and pride, he says, come from within, out of the heart.

He goes north to the region of Tyre. A Gentile woman falls at his feet for her little daughter. He speaks of children and dogs, and she answers, “Yes, Lord. Yet even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” He tells her the demon has gone, and she finds her child on the bed.

A deaf man is brought to him near Galilee. Jesus sighs, says “Ephphatha!” and the man speaks clearly.

The washings Mark describes were customs passed down by the elders, which many Pharisees treated as binding alongside the written law. Mark explains them for readers who may not be Jewish. Jesus’s words about food are read in different ways: many Christians see the end of the Old Testament food laws here, while others stress that his main point is about the heart. His reply to the Syrophoenician woman is difficult, and readers explain it differently. Tyre and Sidon were non-Jewish cities on the coast. See Leviticus 11 and Isaiah 29:13.

Three days with Jesus, and nothing left to eat. He has compassion on the crowd and will not send them home fasting. With seven loaves and a few small fish he gives thanks, and about four thousand eat and are filled, with seven baskets left over. The Pharisees then ask for a sign from heaven, and Jesus sighs deeply and refuses.

In the boat he warns his disciples about the yeast of the Pharisees and of Herod, and they think he means bread. He asks them to remember the baskets from the two feedings. At Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages. The man first says, “I see men, but I see them like walking trees” and then, at a second touch, sees everyone clearly.

On the road to Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks who people say he is, and who the disciples say. Peter answers, “You are the Christ.” Jesus begins to teach that he must suffer, be killed and rise. Peter begins to rebuke him and is rebuked in turn. Jesus calls his followers to take up their cross.

This chapter is the turning point of Mark. Before it the question is who Jesus is; after it, the focus moves toward Jerusalem and the cross. Christ is the Greek form of Messiah, meaning anointed one. Son of Man is Jesus’s usual way of speaking of himself, and it draws on Daniel 7. The healing of the blind man comes just before Peter’s confession, and many readers see a link between gradual sight and gradual understanding. Caesarea Philippi was a largely non-Jewish city north of Galilee.

After six days Jesus leads Peter, James and John up a high mountain, alone. There he is changed before their eyes, his clothes glistening white, and Elijah and Moses are talking with him. Peter, afraid and not knowing what to say, offers to build three tents. A cloud overshadows them and a voice says, “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him.” Then they see only Jesus. On the way down he tells them to say nothing until he has risen from the dead.

At the foot of the mountain a crowd surrounds the other disciples, who could not heal a father’s son. The boy has suffered since childhood. The father pleads, and when Jesus speaks of believing, he cries out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” Jesus heals the boy and raises him up by the hand.

Again Jesus says he will be killed and rise, and they do not understand. They argue about who is greatest, and he sets a child in their midst. Then come sayings on welcoming others, on causing little ones to stumble, and on being salted with fire.

The mountain scene is often called the Transfiguration. Moses and Elijah stand for the law and the prophets in Jewish thought. The boy’s symptoms are described in ways that some readers connect to epilepsy, but Mark presents the cause as an unclean spirit, and the passage gives no medical guidance. Verses 43 to 48 use strong hyperbole about hands, feet and eyes, and Christians differ on how literally to read the warnings about Gehenna, a valley near Jerusalem used as an image of judgment. Some early copies omit verses 44 and 46.

Pharisees come to test him: is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? Jesus points them back to creation, when God made them male and female, and says, “What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.” The disciples turn away parents bringing children, and Jesus is moved with indignation: the Kingdom belongs to such as these.

A man kneels and asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus lists commandments, and the man says he has kept them all. Jesus looks at him with love and says, “One thing you lack.” He is to sell what he has, give to the poor and follow. He goes away sorrowful, for he has great possessions. Jesus says it is hard for the rich to enter the Kingdom, yet all things are possible with God.

On the road up to Jerusalem he says a third time that he will be killed and rise. James and John ask for places of honor, and he teaches that greatness is serving. At Jericho a blind beggar, Bartimaeus, cries out, “Jesus, you son of David, have mercy on me!” and sees.

Divorce was debated among Jewish teachers of the time. Moses’s allowance refers to Deuteronomy 24:1 to 4. Christians differ today on how these words apply to divorce and remarriage, and the passage gives no legal or counseling advice. The needle’s eye saying is a vivid exaggeration, though some later writers tried to soften it. Verse 45 is a key verse for many Christians on the meaning of Jesus’s death, and traditions explain ransom in different ways. Jericho is on the road up to Jerusalem.

Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a young donkey that no one has ridden, and rides it toward Jerusalem. People spread their garments on the road and cut branches from the trees, and cry out “Hosanna!” In the temple he looks around, and since it is evening he goes out to Bethany.

The next day he is hungry. He sees a fig tree with leaves but no figs, and he says that no one will ever eat fruit from it again. Then in the temple he throws out those who buy and sell, and overturns the tables of the money changers. He teaches that the temple was to be “a house of prayer for all the nations” and that they have made it a den of robbers. The chief priests and scribes look for a way to destroy him. By morning the disciples see the fig tree withered from the roots. Jesus says, “Have faith in God” and speaks of prayer and forgiveness.

Later the temple leaders ask by what authority he does these things. He asks them about John’s baptism, and when they will not answer, neither will he.

Mark places the fig tree story on either side of the temple scene, so the two seem to explain each other, though readers differ on how. Money changers exchanged coins for the temple tax, and doves were sold for sacrifices. The temple Jesus clears is the Second Temple, which stood until the Romans destroyed it in the year 70. The quotation about the house of prayer comes from Isaiah 56:7, and the phrase den of robbers echoes Jeremiah 7:11. Hosanna is a cry from Psalm 118.

In the temple, Jesus tells the parable of a vineyard owner who sends servants to collect fruit from tenant farmers. They beat or kill the servants, and finally kill the owner’s son. Jesus says the owner will give the vineyard to others, and the leaders see that the story is aimed at them.

Different groups then try to trap him. Pharisees and Herodians ask about paying taxes to Caesar, and he answers, “Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” Sadducees ask a puzzle about resurrection, and he answers from the story of the bush. A scribe asks for the greatest commandment, and Jesus names love of God and love of neighbor.

He asks how the Christ can be David’s son, warns against scribes who seek honor, and praises a poor widow who gave two small coins.

The vineyard picture comes from Isaiah 5, where Israel is God’s vineyard. The parable is aimed at the temple leaders of that day, and it has sometimes been misused to claim that God rejected the Jewish people as a whole. The text does not say that, and the first followers of Jesus were themselves Jews. The Sadducees were a priestly group who accepted only the first five books of Moses and denied resurrection. The Herodians supported the family of Herod. The great commandments come from Deuteronomy 6:4 and 5 and Leviticus 19:18.

As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple admires the buildings, and Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives, four disciples ask him when this will be and what the sign will be.

Jesus warns them not to be led astray by those who claim to be him. He speaks of wars, earthquakes and famines as the beginning of birth pains, of arrests and trials in which the Holy Spirit will give them words, and of the Good News being preached to all nations. He describes a time of great trouble, the abomination of desolation, and a call to flee, and says false christs will arise.

Then the Son of Man will come in clouds and gather his chosen ones. He says no one knows the day or hour, and he ends by telling them to watch.

This speech is often called the Olivet Discourse. Christians read it in different ways. Some think most of it concerns the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, others see it as describing the end of the age, and many see both together. The phrase abomination of desolation comes from Daniel 9:27 and Daniel 11:31. The words about this generation in verse 30 and the Son not knowing the day in verse 32 are also read in different ways. Birth pains was a common image for the troubles before a new age.

Two days before Passover, the chief priests plot to arrest Jesus quietly. At Bethany a woman pours costly ointment on his head. Some object to the waste, but Jesus says she has prepared his body for burial. Judas Iscariot goes to the chief priests and agrees to betray him.

Jesus shares the Passover meal with the twelve, says one of them will betray him, and gives them bread and the cup, calling them his body and his blood of the new covenant. He predicts that Peter will deny him. In Gethsemane he prays in distress, “not what I desire, but what you desire”, while the disciples sleep.

Judas arrives with an armed crowd and Jesus is arrested. He is tried before the council and answers that he is the Christ, and he is condemned. Peter denies him three times and weeps.

Passover remembers God freeing Israel from Egypt, and the Last Supper is set within it. Christians differ on what happens in the bread and the cup: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed traditions each understand the meal differently. The trial scene has sometimes been misused to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus’s death. The text names a group of temple leaders and the Roman governor in the next chapter, and the church has rejected collective blame. Gethsemane means oil press, a garden on the Mount of Olives. See Psalm 41:9 and Zechariah 13:7.

Early in the morning the council binds Jesus and hands him to Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate asks if he is the King of the Jews, and Jesus answers little. Pilate offers to release a prisoner at the feast. Stirred up by the chief priests, the crowd asks for Barabbas, and Pilate has Jesus flogged and handed over to be crucified.

Soldiers mock Jesus with a purple robe and a crown of thorns. Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross. At Golgotha Jesus is crucified between two robbers, with the charge written above him. People passing by and the chief priests mock him. At the ninth hour he cries out, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and dies. The temple curtain tears in two, and a centurion says this man was the Son of God.

Several women watch from a distance. Joseph of Arimathea asks Pilate for the body and lays it in a rock tomb.

Crucifixion was a Roman punishment used on slaves and rebels, and the charge posted above Jesus was political. Pontius Pilate governed Judea in the 20s of the first century. This chapter has sometimes been used to blame the Jewish people as a whole, and that reading is a serious misuse. The text names the temple leaders, a crowd, and the Roman authorities who carried out the sentence. Jesus’s cry on the cross quotes Psalm 22:1. Christians read the torn curtain in several ways, often as a sign of access to God or of judgment on the temple.

After the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene, another Mary and Salome go to the tomb early on the first day of the week to anoint Jesus’s body. They find the stone already rolled away. Inside, a young man in white tells them Jesus has risen, that he is not there, and that they should tell his disciples and Peter that he goes ahead of them into Galilee. The women flee, trembling and afraid, and say nothing to anyone.

Many early manuscripts end here. Later copies add more verses. They tell of Jesus appearing to Mary Magdalene, to two travelers, and to the eleven, whom he rebukes for unbelief. He sends them to preach to all creation, mentions signs that will accompany believers, and is taken up to heaven.

The ending of Mark is a well-known textual question. The oldest and best known manuscripts stop at verse 8, and verses 9 to 20 appear in later ones. Most Bibles mark this with a note. Churches differ on how to treat the longer ending, but many read it as early and still valued. Verses 17 and 18 about serpents and poison are read in different ways, and some groups have taken them as instructions. Others read them as describing what happened in the early church. See Acts 28:3 to 6 for comparison.
